Chief Metropolitan Magistrate - Ii (New Delhi), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi Cc No. 32/10 Unique Case Id No. 02403R0055922010 Date of Institution: 11.02.2010 Date of reserving judgement: 28.11.2016 Date of pronouncement: 04.01.2017 In re: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector Department of Pfa, Govt. of Nct of Delhi A-20, Lawrence Road Industrial Area, Delhi-110035 ... texts.facts: Accused Judgment: 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules. The acc used is stated to be the vendor cum proprietor of M/s National Bakery from where the food article, that is, 'Vegetable Sauce' was lifted for sampling. 2. As per the complaint, on 24.06.2009, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Suniti Kumar Gupta and Field Assistant (FA) Ashok Kumar under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh.M.S.Vats reached along with their staff at the handcart of M/s. National Bakery, at the corner of Allahabad Bank, Parliament Street, Connaught Place, New Delhi-110001, where the accused was found conducting the business and having stored for sale various food articles. The food officials lifted a sample of Vegetable Sauce, as lying in sealed glass bottles of 500 gm each, bearing no label declaration, from the vendor accused as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 13.07.2009, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the grounds In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/ 1 that it was coloured with synthetic colouring matters 'Tartrazine', 'Sunset Yellow FCF' and 'Ponceu 4 R', that it contained saccharine (artificial sweetner), that the Total Soluble Solids and Acidity contents were less than the prescribed minimum limits, and also that the sample was misbranded because of complete violation of Rule 32 of PFA Rules. Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court on 11.02.2010 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 23 and 29 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act, as well as violation of Section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act read with Rules 24, 47 and 32 of PFA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 11.02.2010. The accused appeared but never filed any application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from the Central Food Laboratory (CFL). 4. The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Suniti Kumar Gupta and PW-2 FI N.N.Sharma. On the basis of their depositions, charge was framed against the accused on 03.07.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, as well as violation of Section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. At the trial, the witnesses examined in pre-charge stage of evidence were recalled for cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, prosecution examined PW-3 Sh. M.S.Vats and PW-4 FA Ashok Kumar in post-charge stage. 5. PW-1, PW-3 and PW-4 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings. All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 24.06.2009 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of three sealed glass bottles of 500 gms each of Vegetable Sauce, dividing it in three parts by taking one sealed bottle as one counterpart, separately sealing and marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C and Raid Report Ex. PW-1/C-1. On the next working day, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/D and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/E. PA report Ex. PW- 1/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-1. He sent letter Ex. PW-1/G to M/s National Bakery at its office at 345-47, Joshi Road, Karol Bagh, New Delhi and received the reply Ex. PW-1/G-1 from the accused herein. The accused sent one label of 'Niraj Vegetable Sauce' claiming that the food article had been purchased by him through a supplier Sh. Raghuraj. Further investigation was conducted by PW-2. He sent letter Ex. PW-2/A to the accused but no reply was received. He sent letters Ex. PW-2/B and Ex. PW-2/C to the STOs and received their replies. He also sent letter Ex. PW-2/F to M/s Bhilwara Food Industry at their Trilokpuri In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/ 2 Office (the manufacturer of Niraj Vegetable Sauce, as per the label furnished by the accused) and received its reply Ex. PW-2/G wherein it denied the sale of its product to the accused and also denied the product in question to be belonging to it. Various letters Ex. PW-2/E, Ex. PW-2/H, Ex. PW-2/H-1 and Ex. PW-2/H-2 were sent to various departments to ascertain the constitution of the firms involved. After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-2/I was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-2/J was filed in the court. Intimation Letter Ex. PW-2/K was sent to the accused along with copy of PA report through post vide receipt Ex. PW-2/L. These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the accused had been falsely implicated or that the sample commodity was not of the same lot or that the intimation letter was not sent at the proper address of the accused or that the manufacturer was intentionally not implicated or that the sample was not taken as per PFA Rules. 6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 21.03.2015 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence. Though accused accepted the proceedings dated 24.06.2009 wherein a sample of vegetable sauce was lifted from him, yet he claimed that the Vegetable Sauce was not for sale but was to be served to the customers alongwith patties, sandwiches etc. He also claimed that there was label declaration on the glass bottles containing the sample. He also stated that he did not accept the price of the sample because the sauce was not for public sale. He took stand that the documents were not read over or explained to him, claiming that his signatures were obtained by FI on several documents. He questioned the PA report asserting that the sample was conforming to standard and the sample had proper label declaration. He denied receiving intimation letter and claimed that he was compelled to sign several documents. Despite given opportunity, accused chose not to lead any evidence in defence.
texts.arguments: 7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 13.07.2009. It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. 8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of witnesses. Ld. Counsel has contended that the PA report and intimation letter were never received by the accused and thus, the right of the accused under section 13(2) PFA Act stood frustrated. It is then argued that the food article was not meant for direct sale and therefore, the matter would not be covered under the PFA Act. It is also submitted that the accused had given representation to the department disclosing the particulars of the manufacturer of the food article who was never implicated in the present case. Ld. Counsel has also argued that there was defect in the sampling method. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be. Section 2(ia)(b) applies there the article contains any other substance which injuriously affects the nature, substance of quality thereof. Ld. Defence Counsel has relied upon judgements titled as Rameshwar Dayal v. State of UP [1996(2) PFA Cases 197], State of Orissa v. Gouranga Sahu [2002 (2) FAC 110] to impress that right under section 13(2) PFA Act is valuable right and it is the duty of the complainant to ensure that such right is not frustrated. In judgement titled as Britannia New Zealand Foods Pvt. v. Director (PFA) [Crl.MC No. 2069/2008, Delhi High Court, dated 01.06.2012], the Hon'ble High Court was dealing with a matter of 'Cheddar Cheese' which was found not conforming to the standards by the PA. The complaint was filed after 18 months of procurement of the sample and it had been argued that the sample was a perishable item and had a shelf life of 9 months, after which filing of the complaint had deprived the accused of his right under section 13(2) of the Act. However, observing that the accused had not applied under section 13(2) of the Act for analysis of second sample by CFL, it was held that the accused could not claim any benefit on that score. The Hon'ble court relied upon the precedent titled as Babu Lal Hargovinddas v. State of Gujarat [AIR 1971 SC 1277], where it was held that "There is also in our view no justification for holding that the accused had no opportunity for sending the sample in his custody to the Director, Central Food Laboratory under Section 13(2) because he made no application to the Court for sending it. It does not avail him at this stage to say that over four months had elapsed from the time the samples were taken to the time when the complaint was filed and consequently the sample had deteriorated and could not be analysed". The Hon'ble Court also considered that in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ghisa Ram [1967 CriLJ 939] as well, the Director had reported that the sample had become highly decomposed and could not be analysed. If in pursuance of the application the part of the sample was sent to the Director and he had reported that the part of the sample was incapable of analysis for the reason that it was decomposed, the accused could perhaps contend that he was deprived of his right to have the sample analysed by the Director on account of the laches of the complainant and that he should be acquitted. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
